slides.title: Reversing the margin decline: restoring a 3% operating margin by FY2028

paragraphs.text: Reversing the margin decline: restoring a 3% operating margin by FY2028
Margin plan for the Board of Directors  ·  February 2027
Presented by Dana Whitfield, CEO, Harlow Fresh Markets
Built only from the internal briefing pack (FY2023–FY2025 actuals). All company figures are synthetic benchmark data. $ figures in millions unless stated.

slides.title: Fix gross margin and delivery economics rather than cutting labor: four quick moves protect the FY2026 covenant, and the full plan restores 3.0% by FY2028

paragraphs.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Fix gross margin and delivery economics rather than cutting labor: four quick moves protect the FY2026 covenant, and the full plan restores 3.0% by FY2028
The decline is mainly in gross margin and e-commerce, not wages

Operating margin fell 2.35 pts (3.37% → 1.02%). Gross margin lost 1.02 pts (promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, private label +0.18) and e-commerce fulfillment 0.84 pts. Store labor cost only 0.30 pts, because 6% higher productivity absorbed most of the 9.4% wage rise.
Management's 8% labor cut would not reach the target

It saves $14.6M, but thinner staffing is linked to higher shrink worth an estimated $5–10M. FY2026 operating income would land at $19–24M against the $20M covenant, and FY2028 margin at only 0.9–1.2%.
A margin-led plan restores ~3.0% for ~$20M of one-time cost

Six levers backed by Harlow's own data (promotions, shrink, labor rebalancing, six lease lapses, private label, delivery fees) take operating income to ~$36M (2.5%) after the 2027 wage step. Three negotiated levers (vendor funding, three lease exits, the delivery contract) add ~$6M, for ~$42M, or 3.0%.
Act first on what is fast, cheap and proven, and hold contingencies

In the first 90 days: roll out the tested delivery fee, cancel money-losing promotions, protect fresh and receiving hours, and reject the 3% delivery-rate rise. FY2026 then reaches ~$24M (about $4M above the covenant). 3.0% has no cushion, so contingency levers are pre-agreed.
Decisions requested today: adopt this plan in place of the 8% labor cut; approve up to $20.5M of one-time spend; schedule a vote on exiting three long-lease stores.
Source: briefing pack Tables 1–6 and §7–9; team analysis. All FY2028 figures are run-rate on the FY2025 sales base.

slides.title: We started with a 'margin, not wages' hypothesis. The evidence supports the diagnosis, but commercial fixes alone reach only ~1.8%, so the answer had to grow

paragraphs.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
We started with a 'margin, not wages' hypothesis. The evidence supports the diagnosis, but commercial fixes alone reach only ~1.8%, so the answer had to grow

Initial hypothesis: the margin fell because of promotions, shrink and loss-making e-commerce growth, not wages, so Harlow can get back to 3% by fixing gross margin and e-commerce alone, with no labor action or store closures.

data: What would have to be true
1  Labor is a minor cause of the decline
Labor explains 0.30 of the 2.35-pt fall (13%). Wage +9.4%, hours per $1,000 of sales −6%
2  Gross-margin erosion comes from drivers Harlow controls
Promo mix (−0.70), shrink (−0.50) and private label (+0.18) add up to the full −1.02 pts
3  The extra promotions are not paying back
38% of events lose money; vendor funding fell 55% → 46%; the 'more expensive' score rose 33% → 41%
Supported, but the response to ValuMart is uncertain
4  E-commerce loses money and repricing fixes it
It loses ~$10.4M on an incremental basis. The fee test recovers ~$2.5M, but delivery still loses $9 per order
Partly: repricing helps but does not fix it
5  Gross-margin and e-commerce fixes alone reach 3%
Promo, shrink, private label and fees add ~$18.8M, but the wage step and delivery rate (−$7.6M) leave ~$26.5M, or 1.8%

paragraphs.text: Revised answer: keep the gross-margin and e-commerce core, and add two levers the first hypothesis left out: (a) targeted labor productivity to absorb the 2027 wage step, rather than an 8% cut, and (b) exits from the weakest stores, starting with the six whose leases lapse by 2027. Vendor funding and the delivery contract close the last gap.
Initial hypothesis set at kick-off, before the analysis. Sources: Tables 1–6, §7–9; calculations on slides 4–16.

slides.title: Gross margin and e-commerce explain 80% of the 2.35-point fall in operating margin; store labor explains only 13%

paragraphs.text: 1  DIAGNOSIS: WHAT DROVE THE DECLINE

What the bridge shows

•  E-commerce (−0.84 pts, 36%): net fulfillment cost went from $5.2M to $18.1M as orders tripled
•  Labor (−0.30 pts, 13%): labor is the largest cost increase in dollars (+$14.3M), which is why it looks like the cause, but most of that just tracked sales
•  Momentum: margin has fallen 1.10 and then 1.25 pts a year. One more year like FY2025 would take margin to about −0.2%, an operating loss, against a $20M covenant

slides.title: Wages rose 9.4%, but 6% fewer hours per sales dollar absorbed most of it, so labor cost only 0.3 points of margin

paragraphs.text: 1  DIAGNOSIS: WHAT DROVE THE DECLINE
Wages rose 9.4%, but 6% fewer hours per sales dollar absorbed most of it, so labor cost only 0.3 points of margin
Wage effect
Productivity effect
Net change in labor % of sales
So what for the plan

•  Wage inflation is real, but it is not the main cause: at FY2023 productivity, FY2025 labor would have cost $193.9M ($18.38 × 7.02 ÷ 1,000 × $1,503M) instead of $181.9M. Harlow has already taken out about $12M through productivity.
•  Productivity gains have not been free: over the same two years shrink rose from 2.1% to 2.6% of sales, and it is highest in the stores with the fewest hours (slide 9).

•  Labor still needs action, because the 2027 minimum-wage step adds ~$7M: +4% on the $181.9M labor bill is $7.3M. The plan offsets most of it through targeted scheduling (−3% net hours, $5.2M) rather than an across-the-board cut.

Source: Table 3. Labor % of sales = hourly wage × hours per $1,000 ÷ 1,000. Effects are calculated in sequence (wage first at FY2023 hours). Table 3 inputs are rounded, so the net (+0.34) differs slightly from Table 1 (+0.30).

slides.title: Promotions (−0.70 pts) and shrink (−0.50 pts) account for the whole 1.02-point gross-margin fall; private label offset only 0.18

paragraphs.text: 1  DIAGNOSIS: WHAT DROVE THE DECLINE
Promotions (−0.70 pts) and shrink (−0.50 pts) account for the whole 1.02-point gross-margin fall; private label offset only 0.18
Gross-margin change by driver, FY2023 → FY2025 (pts of sales)
More promotional sales
Higher shrink
More private label
•  Promotions are the largest single driver: every extra point of promo share costs ~$2.1M a year (1% × $1,503M × 14 pts).
•  Shrink is the second: every 0.1 pt is ~$1.5M a year.
Total explained
Actual change: 26.04% (369.8 ÷ 1,420) → 25.02% (376.1 ÷ 1,503) = −1.02 pts. The three drivers explain all of it, so there is no unexplained cost or price residual left to chase.

Source: Table 2 and notes. Promo effect = change in promo share × 14-pt margin gap; private-label effect = change in share × 12-pt gap; shrink is booked inside gross profit, so it hits margin one for one.

slides.title: The promotion surge is not buying the traffic it was meant to defend: 38% of events lose money and price perception got worse

paragraphs.text: 1  DIAGNOSIS: WHAT DROVE THE DECLINE
The promotion surge is not buying the traffic it was meant to defend: 38% of events lose money and price perception got worse
of FY2025 promotional events lost money, even after counting the extra units they sold
share of promotional markdowns funded by vendors, FY2023 → FY2025. Harlow now pays more of each markdown itself
customers who say Harlow is 'more expensive than other options', despite five more points of promoted sales
FY2025 comparable sales in stores within 3 miles of a new ValuMart vs other stores. Deeper promotions did not protect them
The category team's evidence does not hold up
Implication for the plan
•  The claim: stores with the deepest promotions grew comps 1.8% against 0.2% for the rest (+1.6 pts)
•  Even if all of that gap were caused by promotions, 1.6% × 20% contribution = 0.32 pts of sales. That pays for only 2.3 pts of extra promo share (0.32 ÷ 0.14), and the chain added 5.0 pts
•  It is a correlation: it says nothing about the 38% of events that lose money, or about profit
•  Cut the losing events first. There is a clear profit case, and the risk sits mainly in ValuMart-exposed stores
•  Make vendor funding a condition of running an event, to restore part of the 9-pt funding drop
•  Compete on value through private label (12 pts more margin) and fresh produce, the #1 reason to shop Harlow (58%), not through deeper national-brand markdowns
Source: Table 2 notes; §9 customer survey (n = 3,100) and ValuMart comps; §10 category-team claim. The break-even uses Finance's 20-cent contribution per new sales dollar.

slides.title: Resetting promotions is the largest lever: cutting less than half of the money-losing events is worth ~$6M a year, more if vendors fund the rest

paragraphs.text: 3  RECOMMENDED PLAN: LEVERS AND SIZING
Resetting promotions is the largest lever: cutting less than half of the money-losing events is worth ~$6M a year, more if vendors fund the rest
Three moves
Lever value depends on how much volume is lost

•  Cancel or redesign events that fail the post-event test. Target: promo share back to the FY2023 level of 24%. That means cutting ~17% of promoted sales (5 ÷ 29), well under the 38% of events that lose money.
•  No funding, no feature. Run an event only if the vendor covers at least 50% of the markdown. Each point of funding is worth ~$0.9M.
•  Move the value message to private label and fresh. Private label carries a 12-pt margin premium and answers the 'more expensive' perception without national-brand markdowns.

data: All shifted units sell at regular price

paragraphs.text: •  Shifted sales: 5% × $1,444M = $72.2M. At a 15% loss, $10.8M of sales disappears and $61.4M is sold at regular price
•  Using 20% for lost units is conservative: promoted units earned 14 pts less margin than average

Guardrail for ValuMart stores: phase the cuts in the stores within 3 miles of a ValuMart last, and track their comps weekly against the rest. Keep promotion depth there if the comps gap widens beyond the FY2025 level (−5.3 pts).
Success measures: promo share 29% → 24%; vendor funding 46% → ≥50%; every event passes the post-event profit test before it repeats; comps gap in ValuMart stores no wider than −5.3 pts.

Source: Table 2 and notes. Lever value = (shifted sales − lost volume) × 14 pts − lost volume × 20% contribution, on the $1,444M post-closure base. Vendor pool = 14 pts × 24% × $1,444M ÷ 54% (Harlow's unfunded share), about $90M.

slides.title: Rebalance labor rather than cut it: protecting fresh and receiving hours and trimming 3% where shrink is flat beats the 8% cut by $1–6M

paragraphs.text: 3  RECOMMENDED PLAN: LEVERS AND SIZING
Rebalance labor rather than cut it: protecting fresh and receiving hours and trimming 3% where shrink is flat beats the 8% cut by $1–6M

data: Ring-fence produce rotation and receiving checks; add task hours
Schedule to demand: share of the −3% net hours
Schedule to demand: largest share of the −3%
Ordering and markdown discipline on fresh

paragraphs.text: Compared with the 8% cut, $M a year
•  Rebalancing is still worth $1.4–6.4M more a year than the 8% cut, before counting the cut's untested sales risk
•  −3% net hours is half the pace of FY2023–25 (−6% in two years), so it is achievable with scheduling tools, not layoffs
•  If shrink falls only half as much, the rebalance still nets +$8.1M

How it works in a store: produce rotation and receiving checks become scheduled, protected tasks with their own hours, so they are not skipped on busy days. Q3–Q4 schedules follow the hourly traffic curve. Each store is measured on shrink and labor % together, so neither can be improved at the other's expense.
Source: Tables 3 and 4; §6. Equal quartile sales weights assumed. 13% waste reduction = 0.15 pt ÷ 1.17 pt of waste (45% × 2.6%). Hours are cut in Q3–Q4 stores, where shrink differs by only 0.1 pt.

slides.title: Keep delivery but charge for it: rolling out the tested fee saves $3.0M for a 2% e-commerce sales loss, and the contract renewal can add $0.8M

paragraphs.text: 3  RECOMMENDED PLAN: LEVERS AND SIZING
Keep delivery but charge for it: rolling out the tested fee saves $3.0M for a 2% e-commerce sales loss, and the contract renewal can add $0.8M
Delivery still loses $9.04 per order after repricing, so:
•  Don't grow delivery: keep the 'freeze' for home delivery only; each extra delivered order loses ~$9.
•  Steer to click-and-collect: it loses only $1.64 per order and breaks even if 39% of its sales are new. Pickup capacity is funded in the capital plan.
•  Reject the proposed 3% rate rise in the 2026 renewal and put the contract out to tender. Each 1% of rate is ~$0.1M; −5% instead of +3% is worth $0.8M.
•  Fallback, if renewal fails: limit delivery to dense zones or a higher minimum basket. This keeps delivery 'in some form', as the owners want.

slides.title: Let the six expiring leases lapse (+$4.4M a year, no exit fee) and put the three long-lease stores to a board vote (+$2.2M a year for $7.5M)

paragraphs.text: 3  RECOMMENDED PLAN: LEVERS AND SIZING
Let the six expiring leases lapse (+$4.4M a year, no exit fee) and put the three long-lease stores to a board vote (+$2.2M a year for $7.5M)

data: Chain sales lost (75% of store sales)

paragraphs.text: How to decide
•  Default for the six: do not renew. Before each expiry, renew only if the landlord's rent offer makes four-wall EBITDA positive
•  The three need a board vote: bring the case to the board after two quarters of the commercial fixes. Exit if four-wall EBITDA is still negative
•  Closing all nine would lower chain sales by ~6% but raise margin, because the lost sales carried negative contribution
•  Check ValuMart overlap first. If these stores face ValuMart, the trade-area comps trend (−4.2%) strengthens the case

Why not exit all nine now? the three long-lease stores have the weakest payback in the plan (3.4–4.1 years) and need a board vote. Waiting two quarters costs ~$1.1M of benefit, and it avoids paying $7.5M to exit stores that the commercial fixes might turn around.

Source: Table 6. The pack gives only totals for the nine stores, so a pro-rata split (6/9 and 3/9) is assumed; store-level data should confirm it before each lease decision. Closure running costs (~$0.5M per store) are a team assumption.

paragraphs.text: Contingency levers (not in the plan): promo share down to 22% (+$2.5M); vendor funding back to its FY2023 level of 55% (+$4.4M more); delivery restricted to dense zones; like-for-like sales growth, where each 1% is worth ~$2.8M at 20% contribution. Other uncertainties: how customers react to the labor changes (untested), and whether occupancy and SG&A keep rising faster than sales (+0.2 pt in FY2023–25).

Sensitivities are one at a time on the full plan (3.02%), except the combined downside. Contingency values: promo share to 22% (~$1.26M per pt); vendor funding 50% → 55% (~$0.9M per pt); sales growth at 20% contribution with fixed costs flat.

slides.title: We ask the board for three decisions today and propose five measures to track progress every quarter

paragraphs.text: 4  SEQUENCING, CAPITAL AND RISKS
We ask the board for three decisions today and propose five measures to track progress every quarter
Replace the draft plan
Adopt the margin-led plan and a FY2028 target of at least 3.0% in place of the 8% labor-hour cut. Keep the freeze for home delivery only.
Approve the capital
Up to $20.5M of one-time spend over FY2026–FY2028, with the remaining $4.5M held in reserve and released by the board.
Set up the store vote
Ask management to bring the case for the three long-lease stores to the Q3 FY2026 meeting. Non-renewal of the six expiring leases is the default.

What changes for management: the category team is measured on promotion profit, not comps; the e-commerce team reports contribution including delivery and on an incremental basis; store operations is measured on shrink as well as labor hours. These changes fix the three measurement errors that hid the decline.
KPI baselines are FY2025 values from the briefing pack.

slides.title: A1. The key assumptions behind the numbers, and the choices we made where the pack was silent

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
A1. The key assumptions behind the numbers, and the choices we made where the pack was silent

data: The pack treats FY2026 as the first plan year (labor plan, covenant, capital window) and has no FY2026 actuals. We follow it. If FY2026 has already closed by February 2027, the covenant test is settled and Year 1 shifts to FY2027
Sequencing holds; less time to reach run-rate by FY2028
FY2028 is shown at FY2025 volumes and prices, with no like-for-like growth and no cost inflation except the 2027 wage step
Growth is upside (~$2.8M per 1%); cost drift is downside
+4% applied to the whole store labor bill (conservative: not all staff are on minimum wage)
30% of online sales are new to Harlow (survey), the same for delivery and click-and-collect; the fee test scales chain-wide
C&C per-order economics are sensitive to this share
15% of shifted promo volume is lost, valued at 20% contribution; the 14-pt gap is read as net of vendor funding (this drives the ~$90M vendor-pool estimate)
Quartiles carry equal sales; reallocating hours to Q1–Q2 brings them to Q3 shrink
The six and the three stores are pro-rata shares of the nine-store totals; 25% sales transfer at 12% (past closures)
Store-level data needed before each decision
All except the $7.5M lease exit are team estimates; ~$2M expensed in FY2026
Covenant headroom moves one for one

paragraphs.text: All choices were made without access to management; each should be confirmed before the board meeting.

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
A2. Our e-commerce cost model reproduces Table 1's fulfillment line exactly in every year, so the unit economics can be trusted

data: E-commerce sales as share of total (check vs Table 5)

paragraphs.text: •  Loss per delivered order = contribution on new sales (basket × 30% × 20%) − picking − delivery + fee
•  Losses per order rose each year: delivery cost +$0.90, picking +$0.20 and fees −$0.30, only partly offset by a $2 larger basket
•  The delivered share rising from 45% to 58% mixed the business toward its most loss-making order type
Source: Table 5 (orders, delivered share, unit costs, fees) and Table 1 (fulfillment line). Net = orders × picking + delivered orders × (delivery cost − fee).

slides.title: A3. Run through the same model, management's plan clears the covenant only if shrink barely responds, and misses 3% by $27–32M

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX
A3. Run through the same model, management's plan clears the covenant only if shrink barely responds, and misses 3% by $27–32M

Reading: even in the favorable case the plan passes the covenant by only ~$4M and then erodes as the 2027 wage step arrives, because it leaves promotions, shrink and delivery losses (80% of the decline) untouched. Untested sales losses from service cuts are not included; each 1% of sales costs ~$3M more.

Shrink range: FY2023–25 relation (+0.5 pt shrink for −6% hours) applied to the 8% cut at half and full strength. Wage step on hours after the cut (92% of $181.9M). E-commerce frozen at FY2025 size; no gross-margin actions.
